A synopsis is a short, clear overview of something longer — like a book, film, TV show, play, research paper, or any piece of work — that captures the most important points without going through everything in full detail.

Think of it this way: if a novel is a full painting, the synopsis is a small, accurate sketch of that painting. It's not the whole thing, but it gives you a faithful picture of what the whole thing is about.
What Makes a Synopsis Different From Just "Being Short"

The key is that a synopsis doesn't just shorten something — it preserves the essential shape of it. A good synopsis tells you:

  • What the work is about (the central subject or story)
  • What the main events or ideas are (in order, if it's a story)
  • How it ends or concludes (yes, a synopsis usually includes the ending)

This last point surprises many people. Unlike a teaser or a trailer, a synopsis is not meant to build suspense — it's meant to give a complete, honest picture of the work, just in compressed form.

For a movie: Instead of watching a 2-hour film, you read a synopsis that tells you: a young woman discovers she has powers, goes on a journey, faces a villain, and ultimately saves her city. That's the whole story — compressed.

For a novel: A publisher might ask an author to write a 1-page synopsis of their 300-page book, covering all the major plot points and the ending.

For a research paper: A synopsis tells you what the researcher studied, what method they used, and what they found — without reading all 40 pages.

For a TV show episode: Streaming platforms often show a 2–3 sentence synopsis under each episode so you know what it's about before watching.
The Defining Qualities of a Synopsis

A true synopsis has three qualities:

  1. Brevity — It is significantly shorter than the original work.
  2. Completeness — It covers all the major points, not just the beginning. It doesn't leave out the ending.
  3. Accuracy — It faithfully represents the original. It doesn't add personal opinions, new ideas, or judgments. It just reports what's there.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are close cousins, and people often mix them up, so understanding the differences will sharpen your understanding of "synopsis" itself.

Synopsis vs. Summary
These two are very close and are often used interchangeably in everyday language. However, "synopsis" is more commonly used for narrative works (stories, films, plays) and formal or academic contexts, while "summary" is a more general, everyday word for any shortened version of anything. A synopsis also tends to follow the original structure more faithfully, especially for stories.

Synopsis vs. Abstract
An abstract is used almost exclusively in academic and scientific writing. It appears at the very beginning of a research paper and gives a snapshot of the study. A synopsis can serve a similar purpose but is used much more broadly — for stories, films, and many other works, not just academic papers.

Synopsis vs. Outline
An outline is a list of topics or sections that shows the structure of a work. It tells you what subjects will be covered but doesn't tell you the content or conclusions. A synopsis actually tells you what happens or what is argued — it has real content, not just headings.

Synopsis vs. Review
A review evaluates a work — it gives opinions, ratings, and judgments. A synopsis does not judge. It just describes. A review says "this film is brilliant." A synopsis says "this film is about a detective who solves a decades-old mystery."
How to Use It in a Sentence

• "Before approving the script, the director asked for a synopsis of the entire story."
  • "The back of the book contains a brief synopsis of the plot."
  • "She submitted a synopsis of her research to the conference committee."
  • "I read the synopsis online to decide whether the show was worth watching."
The plural of synopsis is synopses (pronounced sin-OP-seez). This is because the word has Greek roots and follows an older plural pattern, similar to how "crisis" becomes "crises."
A synopsis is a compressed but complete and faithful overview of a longer work — it tells you everything that matters, just without the full detail.
